period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 7 periods = 280 minutes
Total: 7 periods · 4h 40min

periods.activity_title: Incredible India: Reading the Introductory Passage Aloud

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.131): five oral questions on the Hamara Bharat passage.
Let us read (p.132): fill vowels in five identity-word blanks before reading the main text.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads 'Hamara Bharat — Incredible India!' aloud (p.131) with students following. A brief paired exchange invites students to name one feature of Bharat they find most striking before any questioning begins.

Teacher-led discussion using the five 'Let us discuss' questions (p.131): what Bharat is known for, its attractions, unity in diversity, geographical features, and the advice offered. Students respond orally in turns; teacher probes with follow-up.

Pre-reading vowel-completion activity (p.132): teacher writes the five gapped words on the board and students fill in the missing vowels (A, E, I, O, U) individually, then compare with a neighbour. Class confirms each answer aloud.
Quick whole-class consolidation: teacher asks students to explain, in one sentence each, what 'folk art', 'culture', and 'festivals' mean, drawing on the words they just completed.

periods.teacher_notes: The introductory passage centres on Bharat's unity in diversity — wise and heroic people, diverse geography, and shared celebration — which frames every art form that follows. A common pitfall is treating the vowel-completion activity as a spelling drill; redirect students to discuss what each word means in the context of Indian identity.

periods.activity_title: Four Art Forms: Reading and Mapping the Video Conference

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.133): two oral questions on the Ek Bharat, Shreshtha Bharat programme.
Let us discuss (p.136): complete the four-row art-form table with child, state, art, materials.

homework.task_brief: Let us think and reflect I (p.136): fill four blanks on Aipan designs, Dhokra age, coconut craft, Kondapalli materials.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the main 'Kalakritiyon ka Bharat' text (p.133–135) aloud at an unhurried pace, pausing after each child-speaker's turn for students to note the art form name and home state.

Discussion of the two 'Let us discuss' questions on the Ek Bharat, Shreshtha Bharat programme (p.133): what it is, and why it is conducted. Students offer answers orally; teacher builds a shared summary on the board.

Students work in pairs to complete the four-row art-form table (p.136) — child's name, state, art form, and things needed — consulting the text. Pairs share one row each; teacher completes the board version collaboratively.
Teacher sets the fill-in-the-blank task (p.136) as homework, reminding students to re-read the relevant paragraphs before attempting it.

periods.teacher_notes: The main text is structured as four child-speakers in a video conference; helping students track 'who said what about which art form' before the table task prevents confusion later. Students often conflate the materials used across art forms — a brief pause after each speaker during read-aloud reduces this. The four-blank fill-in task (p.136) is left for self-study so that in-class time stays on the richer discussion and table work.

periods.activity_title: Thinking Deeper and Listening to Gakkad Bharta

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect II–IV (p.136): three inferential questions on Aipan, Dhokra wax, and shared features.
Let us listen (p.138): complete five-field notes on Sushil and gakkad bharta after first listening.

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses the three 'Let us think and reflect' questions (p.136) — why Akanksha's family makes Aipan, why wax exits through small openings in Dhokra, and what Kondapalli toys and coconut shell craft share. Students think individually, then discuss in pairs before sharing with the class.

Teacher reads the gakkad bharta transcript (p.162) aloud at a natural pace while students listen with books closed. Students then open notebooks and complete the five-field notes form (p.138): speaker's name, town, state, food item, and vegetables roasted.
Teacher reads the transcript a second time; students verify and correct their notes. Whole class confirms each answer aloud, with teacher writing the correct responses on the board.
Brief oral recap: teacher asks two students to retell in one sentence what gakkad bharta is and where it comes from, reinforcing key listening details.

periods.teacher_notes: The Dhokra wax-exit question (why molten wax drains through small openings when the clay is fired) is the most inferential of the three and often stumps students — prompt them to re-read the lost-wax process description in the prose. For the listening activity, reading the transcript at a natural, unhurried pace is essential; students at this stage benefit from a full second reading before checking answers.

periods.activity_title: Listening for Steps, Then Speaking About Local Art

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.138): complete three-step flowchart for making gakkad bharta after second listening.
Let us speak (p.138): oral presentation on a local art form — name, materials, process.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the gakkad bharta transcript aloud once more. Students fill in the three-step flowchart (p.138) — making gakkad from wheat dough, roasting brinjals and tomatoes for bharta, and the serving method with ghee. Pairs compare flowcharts before a whole-class check.

Teacher models a short oral presentation on one local art form, using the sentence frames on p.138: 'I know about the art form called…', 'They need…', 'To make it, first… after that… next… then… at last…'. Students note the structure and the sequence words used.

Students take turns delivering their own oral presentations (p.138) on a local art form of their choice — painting, rangoli, metal craft, embroidery, music, dance, or drama. Teacher listens and offers brief, encouraging feedback on content and use of sequencing words.
Quick whole-class debrief: teacher names two or three sequence words heard ('first', 'then', 'at last') and asks students why ordering words matter when explaining a process.

periods.teacher_notes: The flowchart step that most often has gaps is Step 3 — the serving method — because students focus on the cooking and miss the crumbling-and-drizzling detail; a targeted second read of that sentence helps. During oral presentations, students who hesitate may need the sentence-frame prompts displayed on the board to build confidence — the NCF note on individual differences in classroom participation applies here.

periods.activity_title: Sequence Words and Present-Tense Verbs in Context

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.137): fill five blanks with sequence words (first, then, after that, next, finally) in 'How I Get Ready for School'.
Let us learn (p.137): make five sentences combining pronouns, verbs, and sentence parts using -s/-es correctly.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly reviews the sequence words (to begin, first, then, after that, next, finally, at last) used by Priyaranjan, Chitra, and Balamurali in the main text, writing them on the board and eliciting one example sentence from the class for each.

Students individually complete the five-blank 'How I Get Ready for School' paragraph (p.137), choosing one sequence word per blank with no repetition. Teacher circulates, then the class reads the completed paragraph aloud together, discussing whether any alternative sequence words could also work.

Teacher explains the -s/-es rule with he, she, and it, using examples drawn from the speakers in the text. Students then construct five sentences (p.137) by combining pronouns, verbs, and sentence-ending phrases from the table, applying the rule where needed. Pairs exchange and check each other's sentences.
Whole-class sharing: three or four students read a sentence each. Teacher highlights on the board any -s/-es choices that need correction, explaining the rule briefly in context.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently use 'firstly' or 'at the beginning' instead of the textbook's register of sequence words — redirect them to the list on p.137 and explain that technical-process writing uses a specific set. The -s/-es rule is best anchored to sentences from the text itself (e.g., 'Aakansha draws geometric designs') rather than invented examples, so the grammar stays connected to meaning.

periods.activity_title: Writing a Paragraph on a Favourite Art Form

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.139): write a five-sentence paragraph giving reasons for liking a chosen art form.

time_bands.activity: Students discuss in pairs which art form — Aipan, Dhokra, coconut shell craft, or Kondapalli — they found most interesting and give one reason each. Teacher takes a quick show of hands so students see the spread of preferences before writing.

Teacher models a short guided-writing plan on the board: sentence 1 (state the art form and reason for choosing it), sentences 2–4 (three specific reasons drawing on process, materials, or cultural significance), sentence 5 (closing reflection). Students note the plan before drafting.

Students draft their five-sentence paragraph independently (p.139), using the art-form details from the main text as evidence. Teacher circulates and offers brief, targeted prompts to students who are stuck on reasons or sentence structure.

Students exchange paragraphs with a partner for a quick peer-response check: Does sentence 1 name the art form? Are there at least three reasons? Is there a closing sentence? Partners give one verbal suggestion each before students revise a sentence or two.
Two volunteers read their revised paragraphs aloud. Teacher affirms strong reason-giving and notes one feature each writer did well.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often write general praise ('it is very beautiful') without grounding reasons in the art form's specific materials or process — prompt them to refer back to the text details (e.g., the lost-wax technique for Dhokra, or the biodegradable quality of coconut shell craft) for concrete reasons. The full drafting and peer-response cycle is kept within this sitting so every student leaves with a complete, revised paragraph.

periods.activity_title: Madhubani Colouring and Ek Bharat Pairing Research

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.139): prepare natural colours from haldi, leaves, geru, flowers, or indigo powder and colour the Madhubani outline.
Let us explore (p.140): find the state paired with your own under Ek Bharat, Shreshtha Bharat and identify cultural practices to explore.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces Madhubani painting as a traditional art form from Bihar, explaining that artists use natural colours on walls (p.139). Students are shown which natural materials produce which colours: haldi for yellow, leaves for green, geru or red flowers for red, flowers for orange, indigo powder for blue.

Students colour the Madhubani outline (p.139) using natural colour samples brought to class or available colour approximations, discussing as they work which colours they are using and why. Teacher circulates, drawing attention to the traditional patterns and encouraging students to name the natural source of each colour they apply.

Teacher reads aloud the Ek Bharat, Shreshtha Bharat programme note (p.140), explaining the state-pairing concept. Students then identify their own state's paired state and briefly discuss in small groups: what cultural practice, food, or art form from that state would they most like to learn about and why?

Each group nominates one spokesperson to share their paired state and one cultural practice they are curious about. Teacher closes by connecting this to the chapter's central idea — that art forms from different states enrich everyone's understanding of Bharat's unity in diversity.

periods.teacher_notes: Natural colour materials (haldi, leaves, flower petals, a pinch of indigo powder) can be gathered from a school garden or kitchen; if unavailable, poster paints or coloured pencils are a valid substitute so the colouring activity still happens. The Ek Bharat, Shreshtha Bharat pairing list (p.140) is the source for state pairs — students who are unsure of their own state's pair should check the table there rather than guess.
materials: Natural colour materials or coloured pencils/poster paints

items.item_stem: Read the passage about the four children's video-conference presentations on regional art forms. Which of the following correctly pairs a child with their home state and art form?

options.label: C
options.text: Chitra — Andhra Pradesh — coconut shell craft

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student has confused the state — Aakansha is from Uttarakhand, not Odisha, though the art form name Aipan is correct.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student has swapped the states of Chitra and Balamurali — coconut shell craft belongs to Kerala, not Andhra Pradesh.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student has reversed the child-state pairing — Balamurali is from Andhra Pradesh, not Kerala, and Kondapalli is the correct art form.

items.source_context: Bharat's identity, unity in diversity, four regional art forms — Aipan, Dhokra, coconut shell craft, Kondapalli.
items.item_stem: The Dhokra craft described by Priyaranjan uses a process called 'lost-wax'. Why is this an appropriate name for the process? Use details from the text to explain your answer in two to three sentences.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The name 'lost-wax' is appropriate because the wax layer applied over the clay figure is literally lost during the process: when the clay-covered figure is fired, the wax melts and drains out through small openings, making way for molten brass to fill its place. The wax is not recovered — it disappears, leaving only the brass shape behind.

items.source_context: Sushil from Jabalpur describes gakkad bharta — a wheat-dough and roasted-brinjal dish from Madhya Pradesh.
items.item_stem: Listen to the description of gakkad bharta given by Sushil. Decide whether each statement below is true or false.

options.text: Sushil is from Bhopal in Madhya Pradesh.
Gakkad is made from wheat dough.
The bharta is made by boiling brinjals and tomatoes.
Gakkad bharta is served with a spoonful of ghee.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. False — Sushil is from Jabalpur, not Bhopal.
2. True — Sushil states that gakkad is made from wheat dough.
3. False — the brinjals and tomatoes are roasted, not boiled.
4. True — Sushil says to drizzle the crumbled gakkad with bharta and add one spoon of ghee.

items.item_stem:
After listening to Sushil's description of gakkad bharta, fill in the blanks to complete the three-step recipe below.

Step 1: Make balls of __________ dough and __________ them on high heat to prepare the gakkad.
Step 2: __________ brinjals and tomatoes, then garnish with chopped onions, coriander, green chillies and salt to prepare the __________.
Step 3: To serve, crumble the gakkad, add some bharta on top, and drizzle with one spoon of __________.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Step 1: wheat / roast. Step 2: Roast / bharta. Step 3: ghee.

items.item_stem: Think of a local art form you know — it could be painting, embroidery, music, dance, or any craft. Describe it to your class: say what it is called, what materials or things are needed, and explain how it is made or performed in the correct order. You have about two minutes to speak.

expected_elements: Names the art form clearly and identifies its region or tradition.
Lists at least two materials or requirements needed.
Describes the process in at least two sequential steps.
Uses at least one sequence word (first, then, next, finally).

items.item_stem: Imagine you are Aakansha, Priyaranjan, Chitra, or Balamurali speaking at the Ek Bharat, Shreshtha Bharat video conference. A student from another state asks you: 'Why should our school learn about your art form? How does it connect us to Bharat's culture?' Respond in about two minutes, giving your opinion with at least two reasons.

expected_elements: Adopts the role of one of the four speakers with their art form and state.
States an opinion on why the art form is worth learning about.
Gives at least two reasons connecting the art form to culture or unity.
Speaks in complete sentences with reasonable fluency and clarity.

Begin with: 'Of all the art forms described in the Ek Bharat, Shreshtha Bharat conference, I think __________ is the most interesting.' Give two specific reasons for your choice, using details about its materials or process from the text. End with a sentence about what the art form tells us about its region.

expected_elements: Names one of the four art forms in the opening sentence.
Provides at least two reasons using text-specific details (material, process, or age).
Closes with a statement linking the art form to its region or culture.
Uses complete sentences with basic punctuation.

items.item_stem: The Ek Bharat, Shreshtha Bharat programme pairs states so that people can learn about each other's culture. Imagine you are writing a short letter to a student in a different state, telling them about one art form from your region that you would like them to know about. Write five to six sentences. You may choose a real local art form or one described in the chapter. Include what it is, how it is made or performed, and why it matters.

expected_elements: Uses an appropriate letter register (greeting, body, closing).
Names the art form and locates it in a state or region.
Describes at least one step in the making or performing process.
States why the art form is meaningful to its community or culture.
Writes in complete sentences with consistent present or simple tense.

items.item_stem: Match each sequence word from Column A with the stage it is best suited to in Column B.
items.visual_stimulus:
Column A — Sequence word | Column B — Stage in a process
First | To mark the very beginning of a process
After that | To continue a step that follows a previous one
Next | To introduce one more step in the middle
Finally | To signal the last or closing step
At last | To show completion after a long series of steps

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: First — beginning; After that — follows previous; Next — middle step; Finally — last step; At last — completion after long series.

answer_key.right: To mark the very beginning of a process
To continue a step that follows a previous one
To introduce one more step in the middle
To signal the last or closing step
To show completion after a long series of steps

items.item_stem:
Each sentence below describes one of the art forms from the chapter. Rewrite each sentence by choosing the correct verb form in brackets. Then write one sentence of your own about any art form from the chapter, using the correct present-tense form of a verb and a sequence word.

1. Aakansha (draw / draws) geometric designs with white rice flour paste.
2. Priyaranjan and his community (make / makes) Dhokra figures from clay and brass.
3. The craftspeople in Kerala (clean / cleans) the coconut shell before shaping it.
4. Balamurali (explain / explains) how soft wood (become / becomes) a Kondapalli toy.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. draws. 2. make. 3. clean. 4. explains / becomes. Student's own sentence should use a verb with correct -s/-es agreement and include at least one sequence word; any art form from the chapter is acceptable.

items.item_stem: Madhubani painting uses natural colours — yellow from haldi, green from leaves, red from geru or red flowers, orange from petals, and blue from indigo powder. Write a short paragraph (four to five sentences) explaining: which two natural colours you would choose for a Madhubani painting and why, what natural sources you would use, and how using natural colours connects Madhubani painting to the traditions described in the chapter.

expected_elements: Names two specific natural colours and their correct natural sources from the chapter.
Gives a reason for choosing each colour (aesthetic, symbolic, or practical).
Links the use of natural materials to the cultural traditions in the chapter.
Writes in coherent sentences with a clear connection to Madhubani painting.

items.item_stem: The Ek Bharat, Shreshtha Bharat programme pairs states to encourage cultural exchange. Find out which state your state is paired with. Then prepare a short project note (a half-page write-up) covering: the name of the paired state, one traditional art form or cultural practice from that state, how that art form or practice is different from or similar to one you learned about in this chapter, and what you would like to learn from the people of that state.

expected_elements: Correctly names the paired state (verified against the p.140 list).
Identifies one real cultural practice or art form from the paired state.
Makes a specific comparison or connection to an art form from the chapter.
Expresses curiosity about the paired state's culture in their own words.
